strengths: Valuable multilingual medical dataset spanning 13 languages including underrepresented ones (Amharic, Yoruba, Swahili) with single verifiable answers and high human verification scores (4.89/5 average)

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 28 baselines, multiple scales (1.5B–72B), and out-of-distribution benchmarks with consistent improvements and strong scaling behavior (57.6%→95.0% language consistency, 28.3%→70.0% accuracy)
Successful joint optimization of language consistency and logical accuracy, addressing a key failure mode in prior multilingual medical systems
Thorough ablation studies isolating contributions of code-switched SFT and GRPO-guided curriculum learning, with detailed per-language performance analysis
Good experimental rigor: IRB approval, native speaker verification, detailed hyperparameters, promised code/dataset release, clear presentation with effective examples
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: code-switching, GRPO, and curriculum learning are established techniques; contribution is primarily engineering rather than methodological innovation

Evaluation relies heavily on proprietary GPT-4o for generation, filtering, and verification with unclear 'separate verifier model' details; binary language consistency metric is overly harsh and doesn't capture acceptable code-switching

Dataset construction uses single source (MedlinePlus) with GPT-4o generation, creating potential systematic bias amplification; filtering removes questions answered by all compact models without justification

Arbitrary design choices lack ablation: reward weights (0.65/0.30/0.05) unexplained, binary language reward not justified, retention ratio α=0.85 unjustified, curriculum based only on Qwen-14B baseline

Shallow error analysis: no breakdown of failure modes, extreme baseline failures unexplained (Gemini 2.5 Pro: 4.33% consistency suggests evaluation issues), high variance across languages not discussed, unclear if very low-resource cases are solvable

Clinical validity concerns: single-answer assumption oversimplifies medicine, claims of 'reliable and equitable' may be overstated, no physician-level validation or USMLE comparison, synthetic verification only
Reproducibility limited despite promises: heavy GPT-4o dependency, no computational cost discussion, hyperparameter justification mostly absent, proprietary models make true reproduction difficult
Missing ablations on curriculum design (only one ordering tested, language-resource vs. complexity-based not compared) and no exploration of alternative reward formulations

Incomplete analysis: no statistical significance testing despite overlapping error bars, only 3 runs, inter-annotator agreement unreported, missing investigation of why multilingual reasoning fails/succeeds

strengths: Addresses important gap in multilingual medical reasoning for low-resource languages with practical healthcare applications
Introduces CUREMED-BENCH with 15,774 instances across 13 languages including underrepresented African languages, verified by medical professionals (4.89/5 rating)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning 28 baselines, multiple model scales (1.5B-32B), and out-of-distribution generalization across three held-out benchmarks
Demonstrates consistent empirical improvements in both language consistency (74.28→85.21% at 7B) and logical accuracy (10.83→54.35%) across model scales
Thorough documentation of methods, hyperparameters, verification protocols, and per-language results supporting reproducibility
Systematic ablation studies isolating contributions of code-switched SFT and curriculum-guided GRPO
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty—combines existing techniques (GRPO from DeepSeek-R1, straightforward curriculum learning by resource tier) without advancing methodology or linguistic understanding; reads as engineering contribution rather than research advancing the field

Significant evaluation concerns: reliance on GPT-4.1 as primary verifier introduces potential systematic bias; binary language consistency metric lacks nuance; 'single verifiable answer' constraint oversimplifies clinical reasoning involving uncertainty and differential diagnoses

Synthetic dataset design limits validity—GPT-4o generation from US-centric MedlinePlus source may not reflect real clinical contexts or global medical practices despite African language coverage; creates potential distribution mismatch

Contradictory design choices: SFT explicitly encourages code-switching (Section 3.2) but RL strictly penalizes it; curriculum tier assignment based on baseline performance creates circularity; reward weighting (0.65/0.30/0.05) lacks justification

Questionable baseline comparisons raising validity concerns: medical-specific models (MedAlpaca-13B, Meditron-70B) show near-zero performance (~0% consistency/accuracy); proprietary models show suspicious patterns (Gemini 2.5 Pro catastrophic failure); suggest evaluation protocol mismatch

Insufficient statistical rigor: only 3 runs reported; no significance testing; suspiciously clean zero-values across multiple models on certain languages; no correction for multiple comparisons across 13 languages and 28 baselines

Weak clinical validation: single-answer paradigm doesn't reflect real clinical decision-making; no expert review of reasoning quality beyond dataset verification; code-switching example (Figure 2) potentially problematic for non-English-fluent clinicians; no failure case analysis

Reproducibility claims overstated despite claims of availability—blank/redacted dataset URL; heavy dependence on proprietary APIs (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1) makes reproduction infeasible for most researchers without significant compute resources

Minimal critical analysis: no error analysis or investigation of failure modes; linguistic phenomena and cross-lingual variation not analyzed; mechanistic understanding of why code-switching helps absent; per-language variance unexplained (e.g., Vietnamese +3.81% logic minimal)

Limited relevance to ACL—primarily applied ML/medical AI rather than computational linguistics; lacks linguistic insights into multilingual reasoning; insufficient focus on language-specific phenomena

strengths: Significant dataset contribution: CUREMED-BENCH uniquely combines 13 languages (including low-resource African languages), open-ended format with verifiable answers, clinical grounding from MedlinePlus, and human verification by experts/native speakers (avg. 4.89/5). Fills a clear gap that no existing benchmark addresses (Table 1).

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 28 baselines across three scales, ablation studies, OOD evaluation on three separate benchmarks (MMedBench, MedExpQA, MedQA), per-language analysis, and analysis of proprietary models.

Well-motivated and linguistically sound methodology: Code-switching during SFT reflects medical practice; curriculum design based on language resource availability (not problem complexity) is novel for multilingual medical reasoning.

Strong and consistent results: Clear improvements across all 13 languages and scales (7B achieves 85.21% consistency/54.35% accuracy); particularly large gains in low-resource languages (e.g., Yoruba +40.86%); scaling behavior shows widening improvements at larger scales.
Excellent reproducibility and ethics: Detailed methodology, hyperparameters, IRB approval, human verification protocols, no patient data, per-language result reporting for transparency.

Clear presentation with effective visualizations: Trade-off analysis (Figure 4) illustrates key contribution; scaling behavior (Figure 5) demonstrates smooth improvement curves; per-language results show uniform gains.
weaknesses: Heavy API dependency limiting reproducibility: Data generation (GPT-4o), filtering (GPT-4o), correctness rewards (closed-source multilingual reward model), and evaluation (gpt-4.1) all rely on proprietary APIs. Prohibits full reproducibility for researchers without access. While acknowledged, proposed solutions (open-source alternatives) remain future work.

Limited methodological novelty: Code-switching supervision is straightforward; GRPO is from prior work (DeepSeek-R1); curriculum learning is standard. Main novelty is problem framing and dataset rather than technical innovation. Combination is sensible but incremental.

Evaluation methodology concerns: LLM-as-judge relies on GPT-4o which may bias toward fluent but incorrect outputs; no inter-rater agreement metrics for the human verification scores; binary correctness judgment (Eq. 1) may miss nuanced reasoning; no robustness analysis varying the judge.

Incomplete analysis of core design choices: Curriculum tiers based on single baseline model (Qwen2.5-14B) without justification; reward weights (0.65, 0.30, 0.05) appear arbitrary with no ablation studies; code-switching claim ('use most effective language') unsupported by analysis of actual intermediate languages used.

Modest absolute performance and persistent gaps: 54.35% accuracy at 7B is still far from clinical reliability; 37% performance gap between high-resource (French 77.86%) and low-resource (Yoruba 40.86%) languages persists despite method; unclear if accuracy sufficient for practical clinical deployment.

Limited error analysis and qualitative insights: No systematic error analysis showing failure modes; only one qualitative example (Figure 3); no investigation of why curriculum learning helps mechanistically; no analysis of which medical conditions are harder or how reasoning chain length affects performance.

Small per-language test sets: Only ~243 test instances per language (15,774 * 0.2 / 13), limiting statistical confidence in per-language claims. Language distribution uneven (French 13.5%, Bengali 2.9%).

Experimental design fairness concerns: CURE-MED trained specifically on CUREMED-BENCH while baselines are general-purpose or different-domain; comparison becomes apples-to-oranges. No statistical significance testing despite reported standard deviations. No computational cost analysis for RL vs. scaling alternatives.

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine gap in multilingual medical reasoning with dual focus on logical correctness and language consistency
High-quality, clinically-grounded dataset (CURE-MED-BENCH) with 15,774 instances across 13 languages including low-resource ones, human verification (4.89/5 rating), and IRB approval
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 28 baselines, multiple scales (1.5B-72B), OOD evaluation on 3 additional benchmarks, thorough ablations, and per-language analysis
Sound curriculum design motivated by empirical observation that models achieve better rewards on high-resource languages, enabling stable transfer to low-resource settings
Strong empirical results with consistent gains across all scales and languages, particularly impressive improvements in low-resource settings (e.g., 0.95→17.14% on Amharic)
Effective remedy for identified failure modes: clinically plausible but incorrect reasoning, language drift, and low-resource degradation
Good reproducibility documentation with detailed prompts, hyperparameters, verification protocols, and results with standard deviations
weaknesses: Same-model judge bias: GPT-4o used for both synthetic data generation and reward verification, creating potential systematic biases despite mention of separate verification model
Heavy API dependence limits full reproducibility and accessibility; acknowledged limitation but deferred to future work
Limited technical novelty: curriculum learning and GRPO are established; primary contribution is engineering their combination with language-aware design—incremental rather than novel
Concerning absolute performance on low-resource languages (Swahili 7B: 35.71%, Amharic 7B: 17.14%) may limit clinical utility despite claims of 'reliable and equitable' reasoning
Circular curriculum definition: language tiers defined by Qwen2.5-14B baseline performance; transfer to other model families not demonstrated
Binary language consistency reward (Eq. 2) may be overly strict; natural code-switching in medical contexts not captured
Missing critical ablations: no sensitivity analysis for reward weights (0.65/0.30/0.05), retention ratio α=0.85, or curriculum granularity
LLM-as-judge evaluation limitations underexplored: no inter-rater agreement reported, no human evaluation of clinical soundness beyond initial dataset verification
Dataset synthetic; uneven language coverage (French 13.5% vs Bengali 2.9%); limited to single-answer diagnostic QA without real clinical complexity (longitudinal care, multimodal evidence)
Incomplete analysis: no investigation into why certain languages/topics harder beyond resource availability; no cross-model generalization demonstrated (all Qwen2.5)

strengths: Comprehensive multilingual medical reasoning dataset (CUREMED-BENCH) spanning 13 diverse languages including underrepresented African languages, with rigorous human verification by medical professionals (4.89/5 quality rating)
Extensive empirical evaluation across 28 baselines, multiple model scales (1.5B-32B), with consistent improvements in both language consistency (94.96% at 32B) and logical accuracy (70.04% at 32B)
Well-motivated curriculum design based on language resource availability rather than task complexity, with clear failure mode analysis (Section F) justifying design choices
Thorough experimental documentation including hyperparameters, training details, per-language analysis, OOD generalization tests, and ablation studies demonstrating systematic evaluation
Thoughtful two-stage approach combining code-switching-aware SFT with curriculum-guided GRPO that jointly optimizes logical correctness and language fidelity
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: code-switching, GRPO, and curriculum learning are all existing techniques; primary contribution is combination/application rather than technical innovation for top-tier venue

Significant evaluation methodology concerns: (1) heavy dependence on proprietary GPT-4o API for both generation and evaluation raises reproducibility risks; (2) oversimplified binary language consistency metric (Eq. 2) doesn't capture nuanced multilingual quality; (3) no inter-annotator agreement or human evaluation of final model outputs; (4) 'single verifiable answer' assumption may oversimplify clinical reality

Incomplete ablations obscure component contributions: missing ablations for each reward component (λ_acc, λ_lang, λ_fmt weights), code-switching necessity, RL algorithm choice, and critical hyperparameter α=0.85; unclear which components drive improvements

Reproducibility red flags: (1) repository URL missing ('available at .'); (2) requires 130-250 GPU-hours on 8 A100s; (3) verification relies on proprietary gpt-4.1 API with no fallback; (4) vulnerable to future API changes

Dataset limitations: (1) limited test scale (~240 examples per language after 80/20 splits); (2) uneven language distribution (French 13.5% vs Bengali 2.9%); (3) US-centric (MedlinePlus only); (4) no statistical significance testing despite reporting standard deviations

Questionable baseline comparisons: some baselines perform far below expectations (Meditron-70B at 0.21% consistency), suggesting evaluation compatibility issues; unfair comparison as CURE-MED has access to in-domain training data others lack

Modest improvements for stated low-resource focus: despite emphasis on low-resource languages, logical accuracy remains low (Yoruba 40.86%, Amharic 17.14%, Swahili 35.71% at 7B), suggesting fundamental challenges unaddressed

Key design choices lack justification: arbitrary reward weights (0.65/0.30/0.05), no evidence code-switching is necessary, no comparison of RL algorithms (PPO, DPO vs GRPO), missing curriculum ordering ablations

strengths: Addresses critical gap in multilingual medical reasoning with strong empirical evidence of two recurring failure modes (logical inaccuracy and language drift) that are well-motivated and documented

CUREMED-BENCH is a substantial and well-curated dataset (15,774 instances, 13 languages including underrepresented ones) grounded in clinically validated sources with rigorous human verification (4.89/5 avg rating) and IRB approval

Comprehensive experimental validation: 28 baselines, per-language analysis, ablations showing necessity of code-switching SFT and curriculum-guided RL, out-of-distribution generalization, and curriculum ordering ablation

Well-motivated methodology: code-switching during reasoning while enforcing target-language output is intuitive; curriculum progression from high-to-low-resource languages grounded in observation about reward stability

Strong, consistent empirical results across all scales: CURE-MED-7B achieves 85.21% consistency + 54.35% accuracy; particularly large gains in low-resource languages (Amharic 0%→64.76%, Yoruba 0%→77.42%)
Thorough documentation including detailed prompts, hyperparameters, human verification protocols, failure mode analysis, and per-language breakdowns supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Medical correctness evaluation critically depends on LLM-as-judge (GPT-4o) without independent physician verification of model outputs—a notable gap for claims about medical reliability and clinical validity

Heavy reliance on proprietary APIs (GPT-4o) for generation, verification, and evaluation creates reproducibility and accessibility barriers; acknowledged desire to provide open-source alternatives but not delivered
Binary language consistency metric is crude and doesn't distinguish minor code-switching during reasoning from major language mixing; unclear how metric handles code-switching allowed in SFT stage
Reward design choices (weights 0.65/0.30/0.05, binary language/format rewards) appear arbitrary with limited ablation; no sensitivity analysis on critical hyperparameters
Curriculum tier assignments based on single reference model (Qwen2.5-14B); different model architectures may benefit from different orderings, and only reverse-order ablation tested

Out-of-distribution generalization sometimes modest (e.g., MedQA improvements of only 1% at 32B on Simplified Chinese); unclear transfer to truly novel clinical scenarios beyond benchmark distributions
No independent human evaluation of model outputs; dataset verification (4.89/5) is for synthetic Q&A pairs, not model-generated outputs—essential for medical domain credibility

Missing analyses: no investigation of what linguistic/medical features learned in each curriculum phase, limited failure mode co-occurrence analysis, and no discussion of potential negative impacts (medical misinformation risks)
Proprietary model comparisons (Table 8) only in zero-shot setting; claims would strengthen if showing CURE-MED wins even when proprietary models are fine-tuned
Substantial computational cost (130-250 GPU-hours on 8 A100s) limits reproducibility without quantified comparison to baseline efficiency
